question_text: The radius of a circle is measured as $7\text{ cm}$, rounded to the nearest centimetre.

subparts.stem: Use this measurement to estimate the area of the circle.
Find the boundary values for the area of the circle.

mark_breakdown.desc: Identifying radius bounds $6.5\text{ cm}$ and $7.5\text{ cm}$
Calculating lower and upper area boundaries

subparts.solution:
The radius length could be from $6\frac{1}{2}\text{ cm}$ to $7\frac{1}{2}\text{ cm}$.
$\therefore$ the lower boundary of the area is $\pi \times (6\frac{1}{2})^2 = 42.25\pi\text{ cm}^2 \approx 133\text{ cm}^2$
and the upper boundary of the area is $\pi \times (7\frac{1}{2})^2 = 56.25\pi\text{ cm}^2 \approx 177\text{ cm}^2$.

ai_explanation.concept_rule: Measurements given to the nearest unit have bounds of $\pm 0.5$. Lower and upper area bounds are obtained by evaluating area at these radius bounds.
ai_explanation.common_pitfalls: Using $\pm 1$ as the boundary interval instead of $\pm 0.5$.

subparts.stem: Hence find the maximum percentage error in the estimate.

mark_breakdown.desc: Calculating percentage error for both extreme exact values
Identifying the maximum percentage error as approximately $16.0\%$

subparts.solution:
If the exact area $V_E$ was $42.25\pi\text{ cm}^2$, the percentage error $= \frac{|V_A - V_E|}{V_E} \times 100\%
= \frac{|49\pi - 42.25\pi|}{42.25\pi} \times 100\% \approx 16.0\%$
If the exact area $V_E$ was $56.25\pi\text{ cm}^2$, the percentage error $= \frac{|V_A - V_E|}{V_E} \times 100\%
= \frac{|49\pi - 56.25\pi|}{56.25\pi} \times 100\% \approx 12.9\%$
$\therefore$ the maximum percentage error in the estimate $\approx 16.0\%$.

ai_explanation.concept_rule: The maximum percentage error occurs when the relative difference $\frac{|V_A - V_E|}{V_E}$ is maximized, typically at one of the extreme boundary values of $V_E$.
step_by_step: Compare the two values; the maximum is $\approx 16.0\%$.
ai_explanation.common_pitfalls: Assuming the upper bound of area gives the larger percentage error without calculating both, ignoring the effect of the smaller denominator.
